abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for understanding context-dependent meaning in conversational systems, fundamentally reconceptualizing how dialogue systems process implicit semantic relations. Current approaches treat dialogue context as a linear sequence of utterances, failing to capture the hierarchical and recursive nature of conversational implicature. We propose the Contextual Resonance Theory (CRT), a formal model grounded in game-theoretic semantics that treats dialogue as a collaborative inference process where meaning emerges from mutually shared assumptions. Our framework introduces formal operators for modeling presupposition projection, implicature cancellation, and epistemic updates within a unified mathematical structure. We prove theoretically that CRT subsumes existing context models while providing superior explanatory power for phenomena such as ellipsis resolution, indirect speech acts, and non-literal interpretation. Experiments on benchmark dialogue corpora demonstrate that formalizing context representation according to CRT principles yields substantial improvements in machines' ability to track conversational state and resolve referring expressions. This work opens a new research direction at the intersection of computational linguistics and formal semantics, offering a principled alternative to purely data-driven approaches for dialogue system development.

We present a theoretically grounded analysis of attention mechanisms in neural machine translation that significantly extends current understanding of how transformer architectures capture linguistic dependencies. While prior work has demonstrated the empirical success of multi-head attention, theoretical explanations for why certain attention patterns emerge remain limited. We develop a formal analysis framework based on spectral graph theory to characterize the expressive capacity of attention configurations, proving that current implementations systematically underutilize available attention heads for capturing long-range syntactic relations. Our analysis identifies specific architectural modifications that can enhance the model's ability to represent non-projectively ordered constituents—a known weakness in dependency parsing. We introduce the Linguistically-Informed Attention Decay (LIAD) mechanism, which imposes biologically-inspired constraints on attention weight distribution based on established principles of syntactic dependency length minimization. Experiments on standard WMT benchmarks demonstrate that LIAD-enabled transformers achieve statistically significant improvements in translation quality, particularly for languages with flexible word order. This work provides both theoretical insight into attention mechanisms and practically applicable modifications for improving machine translation systems.

This paper presents a fundamentally new architecture for real-time multilingual question answering systems that breaks from the conventional pipeline design. Traditional QA systems process queries sequentially through language identification, translation, retrieval, and answer generation stages, accumulating errors and introducing unacceptable latency for interactive applications. We introduce the Unified Multilingual Reasoning Engine (UMRE), a novel architecture that performs cross-lingual understanding through a shared symbolic representation layer, eliminating the need for explicit translation. The system employs learnable interlingual concepts that capture semantic invariants across languages, enabling direct reasoning over multilingual knowledge bases without intermediate translation. Key innovations include a dynamic vocabulary binding mechanism that maintains coherent multilingual attention and a streaming inference protocol that enables sub-second response times while processing arbitrarily long context documents. We implement UMRE as an open-source framework supporting twelve languages with documented APIs for seamless integration into existing applications. Evaluation on MLQA and XQuAD benchmarks demonstrates that the system achieves competitive accuracy with state-of-the-art pipeline approaches while reducing inference latency by 60%. This work establishes a new paradigm for building language-agnostic QA systems that prioritize both accuracy and responsiveness.

We present an enhanced system design for aspect-based sentiment analysis that substantially improves computational efficiency while maintaining high accuracy across diverse text domains. Existing approaches to aspect-level sentiment extraction typically require multiple model passes or complex multi-task architectures, making them impractical for real-time applications processing high-volume user-generated content. Our system introduces a novel hierarchical attention framework that jointly performs aspect term extraction, aspect categorization, and sentiment classification within a single unified model. The architecture employs a coarse-to-fine attention mechanism where first-stage global attention identifies candidate aspects and second-stage specialized attention assigns sentiments, enabling significant parameter sharing while maintaining task-specific discriminative capacity. We develop an optimized inference pipeline with batching strategies and model quantization that reduces memory footprint by 40% without accuracy degradation. The system achieves state-of-the-art performance on SemEval 2014 Task 4 and 2016 Task 5 benchmarks, with particularly notable improvements on low-resource domains through effective transfer learning. We release the complete implementation with comprehensive documentation, enabling practitioners to deploy high-quality aspect-based sentiment analysis at scale.
